blocks.content: A monitor is a high level synchronization construct that bundles shared data together with the procedures that operate on it, and guarantees that only one thread can be actively executing any of those procedures at a time. There are no manual lock or unlock calls for the programmer to write. The mutual exclusion is automatic and structural, enforced by the construct itself rather than by programmer discipline.

This chapter builds on the mutex and the semaphore, the two lower level tools used to protect shared data. It explains why monitors exist, how a monitor is structured, how condition variables let a thread wait for a specific state, and how the classic bounded buffer problem looks when solved with a monitor.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408558643-860265592.png
1. What Is a Monitor

A monitor packages three things into one unit: shared variables, the procedures allowed to touch them, and a built in rule that only one thread may be inside any of those procedures at any moment. Code outside the monitor cannot read or write the shared variables directly. It can only call the monitor procedures, and the monitor itself enforces exclusive access.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: A monitor is shared data plus the operations on it plus an automatic guarantee that only one thread runs inside those operations at a time.
No explicit lock or unlock

With a mutex, the programmer writes lock() before touching shared data and unlock() after. With a monitor, that locking happens automatically the moment a thread calls one of the monitor procedures, and it is released automatically when the procedure returns. The programmer never writes a lock call by hand.

blocks.content: 2. Why Monitors Exist

Raw mutexes and semaphores are powerful, but they depend entirely on the programmer using them correctly every single time. A forgotten unlock call, an unlock in the wrong order, or an accidental double unlock can silently break an entire program. These mistakes are easy to make and hard to spot in review.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408558643-139209941.png

blocks.title: The core idea
blocks.content: A monitor turns mutual exclusion from a matter of programmer discipline into a property enforced by the language or runtime itself. The bug simply cannot happen, because there is no manual step to forget.

This does not make monitors strictly more powerful than semaphores. A monitor can even be built out of a mutex and condition variables underneath. What changes is safety: the low level details are handled once, correctly, inside the monitor implementation, instead of being repeated imperfectly at every call site.
3. The Structure of a Monitor

Picture a monitor as a box. Inside the box sit the shared variables and the procedures that operate on them. Outside the box, an entry queue holds every thread that wants in but cannot get in yet, because someone else is already inside.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408558644-272927967.png
Only one thread inside at a time
blocks.text: Only one thread inside at a time

blocks.content: When a thread calls a monitor procedure, it first checks whether the monitor is occupied. If it is free, the thread enters and runs. If it is occupied, the thread joins the entry queue and sleeps until the monitor becomes free. When the running thread finishes its procedure, the monitor picks the next thread from the entry queue.

4. Condition Variables: wait and signal

A monitor alone only guarantees mutual exclusion. It says nothing about a thread that gets inside but finds it is not yet the right moment to proceed, for example a consumer that finds an empty buffer. Condition variables are the mechanism a monitor uses to let a thread step aside and wait for a specific condition to become true. The sibling Condition Variables chapter covers them in full depth; this section introduces just enough to make monitors useful.
wait()

When a thread inside the monitor calls wait() on a condition variable, it gives up its exclusive access and goes to sleep on that condition variable queue. Giving up the monitor is what allows another thread to enter and eventually change the state the sleeping thread is waiting for.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408558644-381475452.png
signal() or notify()

When a thread inside the monitor changes the state so that a waiting condition becomes true, it calls signal(), also called notify() in some languages, on that condition variable. This wakes exactly one thread sleeping there. The woken thread does not run immediately; it must wait for the monitor to be free again before it can continue.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408558644-180011873.png
5. Worked Example: Bounded Buffer with a Monitor
blocks.text: 5. Worked Example: Bounded Buffer with a Monitor

blocks.content: The bounded buffer, also called the producer consumer problem, is the classic showcase for monitors. A fixed size buffer sits inside a monitor. Producers must wait when the buffer is full, and consumers must wait when it is empty. Two condition variables capture these two situations.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408558644-409744162.png
blocks.alt: Worked Example: Bounded Buffer with a Monitor

blocks.content: Producer adds an item
A producer calls deposit(). If the buffer is full, it waits on notFull. Once space exists, it adds the item and calls signal() on notEmpty, waking a consumer that may be waiting for data.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408558644-281392939.png
Consumer removes an item

remove() is the mirror image. A consumer waits on notEmpty when the buffer is empty, takes an item once one exists, and signals notFull so a waiting producer can add more. Neither side ever touches count or buffer directly from outside these two procedures.
6. Monitors vs Semaphores

Semaphores and monitors both coordinate access to shared resources, but they sit at different levels of abstraction. A semaphore is a low level counter that any thread can increment or decrement; a monitor is a high level construct that hides the counting and locking inside procedure calls.

7. Real Language Support

Monitors are not just a textbook idea. Java synchronized keyword, together with the built in wait(), notify(), and notifyAll() methods on every object, is a direct and widely used implementation of monitor style synchronization. A synchronized method behaves exactly like a monitor procedure: only one thread can be inside it for a given object at a time.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408559199-485980190.png
8. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle
blocks.text: 8. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle

blocks.content: Spurious wakeups: signal versus a loop
blocks.text: Spurious wakeups: signal versus a loop

blocks.content: A thread that wakes up from wait() cannot assume the condition it was waiting for is still true. Another thread may have gotten to the monitor first and consumed the very thing it was waiting for. This is why the condition must always be rechecked in a while loop, never assumed true after a single if check.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408559201-926961650.png
blocks.alt: Spurious wakeups: signal versus a loop

blocks.content: Always wait inside a while loop that rechecks the actual condition, never inside an if that assumes waking means the condition is true.
Interview angle

blocks.title: What interviewers listen for
blocks.content: Be ready to explain that a monitor gives automatic mutual exclusion where a semaphore does not, that condition variables are how a monitor waits for a state rather than just a lock, that Java synchronized plus wait and notify is a real world monitor, and that the wait call always belongs inside a while loop because of spurious wakeups.
